questions.s: Concerning the axillary artery and vein (Last's):
o: With the arm at the side the third part of the axillary artery is clasped by the two roots of the median nerve
In abduction and lateral rotation the artery straightens. (Last's p. 66)
The posterior circumflex humeral artery passes through the triangular space
It passes through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve. (Last's p. 66)
The posterior circumflex humeral is much larger than the anterior
It anastomoses with the profunda brachii. (Last's p. 66)
The axillary vein has a sheath like the artery
There is no axillary sheath around the vein. (Last's p. 66)
No branches arise from the divisions of the brachial plexus
Branches come from roots, trunks and cords. (Last's p. 67)
The lateral, medial and posterior cords give 5, 5 and 3 branches
They give 3, 5 and 5. (Last's p. 67)
The cords embrace the second part of the axillary artery
They enter above its first part and branch around its third. (Last's p. 66)
The divisions of the plexus lie in the posterior triangle
Roots between scalenes, trunks in the triangle, divisions behind the clavicle, cords in the axilla. (Last's p. 67)
The dorsal scapular nerve arises from C5 and pierces scalenus medius
It usually supplies levator scapulae too. (Last's p. 67)
The nerve to subclavius passes behind the subclavian vessels
It passes in front of the trunks and vessels. (Last's p. 67)
The C7 root of the long thoracic nerve descends in front of scalenus medius
C5 and C6 pierce the muscle. (Last's p. 68)
The long thoracic nerve runs in front of the midaxillary line
It runs posterior to the midaxillary line. (Last's p. 68)
The lateral pectoral nerve supplies pectoralis minor via its communication with the medial pectoral
It has no cutaneous branch. (Last's p. 68)
The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm is the smallest branch of the plexus
The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm is the smallest. (Last's p. 68)
The ulnar nerve receives C7 fibres from the lateral cord in over 95%
These supply flexor carpi ulnaris. (Last's p. 68)
The medial pectoral nerve arises in front of the axillary artery
It arises behind it. (Last's p. 68)
The lower subscapular nerve is larger than the upper
It gives a twig to teres major. (Last's p. 69)
The thoracodorsal nerve is C5, 6
It is C6, 7, 8. (Last's p. 68)
The axillary nerve supplies nothing in the axilla
Its origin is higher than usually imagined. (Last's p. 69)
The posterior circumflex humeral vessels lie above the axillary nerve in the quadrangular space
They lie below it. (Last's p. 69)

questions.s: Concerning the axillary and radial nerves (Last's):
o: The posterior branch of the axillary nerve supplies teres minor
Then becomes the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm. (Last's p. 69)
The radial nerve is C5–8 only
Last's gives it as C5, 6, 7, 8, T1. (Last's p. 69)
The nerve to the medial head of triceps accompanies the ulnar nerve
It arises before the radial nerve leaves the axilla. (Last's p. 69)
The radial nerve leaves the axilla through the quadrangular space
Through the triangular space below teres major. (Last's p. 69)
Part of brachialis is supplied by the radial nerve
Evidence it developed partly in the extensor compartment. (Last's p. 80)
The lateral intermuscular septum is pierced by the ulnar nerve
The radial nerve and anterior descending profunda branch pierce it; the ulnar pierces the medial septum. (Last's p. 80)
The basilic vein pierces the deep fascia opposite the deltoid insertion
About mid-arm. (Last's p. 80-81)
The median nerve crosses behind the brachial artery
It crosses obliquely in front, from lateral to medial. (Last's p. 81)
The median nerve has no muscular branches in the arm
Unless the nerve to pronator teres arises high. (Last's p. 81)
The ulnar nerve supplies the elbow joint from the arm
Its articular twig arises in the groove behind the medial epicondyle; it gives no branch in the arm. (Last's p. 82)
The ulnar nerve pierces the medial septum with the superior ulnar collateral artery
And the radial branch to the medial head of triceps. (Last's p. 82)
The supratrochlear nodes drain to the apical axillary nodes
They drain to the lateral axillary group. (Last's p. 82)

questions.s: Concerning triceps and the radial nerve (Last's):
o: Triceps receives four radial branches, two to the medial head
In order: long, medial, lateral, medial. (Last's p. 83)
The radial nerve lies on bone along the whole radial groove
It touches periosteum only at the lateral edge, at the lower end. (Last's p. 83)
The branch to anconeus runs through the medial head of triceps
(Last's p. 83)
Last's says the medial head of triceps is aptly named
It would be better called the deep head; the long head is actually medial. (Last's p. 82)
The radial nerve can be rolled on the humerus a third of the way from deltoid tuberosity to lateral epicondyle
(Last's p. 83)
Only the posterior branch of the profunda brachii pierces the lateral septum
Only the anterior branch does. (Last's p. 83)
Mid-shaft humeral fractures seldom paralyse triceps
Its branches arise high. (Last's p. 83)
The superficial radial nerve lies on the ulnar side of the radial artery
It lies on the radial side under brachioradialis. (Last's p. 94)
The elbow capsule is not attached to the radius
It attaches to the annular ligament. (Last's p. 84)
The posterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament is the strongest
The anterior band is the strongest. (Last's p. 84)
The ulnar nerve lies on the middle (oblique) band of the ulnar collateral ligament
(Last's p. 84)
The ulnar nerve is more easily compressed against the humerus than the coronoid
Last's says it is more easily compressed against the coronoid. (Last's p. 94)

questions.s: Concerning the median nerve in the forearm (Last's):
o: The median artery arises from the anterior interosseous
It was the original axial artery. (Last's p. 94)
The anterior interosseous nerve has a small cutaneous branch
It has none. (Last's p. 94)
The median nerve is overlapped at the wrist by palmaris longus from the ulnar side
It is flattened there. (Last's p. 94)
The palmar branch of the median arises in the carpal tunnel
It arises just above the flexor retinaculum. (Last's p. 94)

questions.s: Concerning the ulnar nerve and radioulnar joints (Last's):
o: The branch to flexor carpi ulnaris carries C7 fibres
The branch to FDP carries C8 and T1. (Last's p. 94)
The dorsal ulnar nerve supplies the nail beds of the ulnar one and a half fingers
It supplies proximal to the nail beds. (Last's p. 94)
The quadrate ligament has constant overall tension in all positions
Its fibres criss-cross. (Last's p. 95)
The interosseous membrane is taut in supination
It is taut in pronation, lax in supination. (Last's p. 95)
Extensor carpi radialis brevis is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve before it pierces supinator
Sometimes by the superficial radial. (Last's p. 100)
Anconeus is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve
By a radial branch from the radial groove, through triceps. (Last's p. 100)
The branch to supinator leaves the posterior interosseous nerve in the cubital fossa
Supinator is C5, 6. (Last's p. 101)
The posterior interosseous nerve has a cutaneous branch on the dorsum of the wrist
It has no cutaneous branch; it ends in a nodule supplying the wrist. (Last's p. 103)
Supinator is the prime mover of supination only with the elbow fully extended
Biceps is the powerful supinator. (Last's p. 101)
Hammer thumb after Colles' fracture is due to the tendon wearing on fragments
It is due to occlusion of anterior interosseous branches supplying the EPL tendon. (Last's p. 102-3)
The extensor indicis tendon lies on the ulnar side of the extensor digitorum tendon
(Last's p. 103)
The extensor retinaculum is attached to the ulna
It is attached to the radius and to the pisiform and triquetral, not the ulna. (Last's p. 103)
The posterior interosseous artery passes above the interosseous membrane and below the oblique cord
(Last's p. 103)
The posterior interosseous artery supplies the whole extensor compartment to the wrist
It is exhausted at the lower border of extensor indicis; the anterior interosseous supplies below. (Last's p. 103)
The cephalic vein begins in the snuffbox
From the radial side of the dorsal venous network. (Last's p. 103)
Abductor pollicis longus has a radial origin proximal to its ulnar origin
The ulnar origin is more proximal. (Last's p. 102)
In the carpal tunnel the middle and ring superficialis tendons lie in front of index and little
(Last's p. 108)
In the carpal tunnel all four profundus tendons are separate
Only the index tendon is separate. (Last's p. 108)
The common flexor sheath is reflected from the radial side of the tendons
For arterial access. (Last's p. 108)
The median nerve lies medial to the superficialis tendon to the middle finger
It lies lateral to it, between it and flexor carpi radialis. (Last's p. 109)
Flexor pollicis brevis has the most variable nerve supply of any muscle
Median, ulnar, or both. (Last's p. 109-110)
Last's names fibres inserted into the ulnar sesamoid flexor pollicis brevis
Those belong to adductor pollicis or the first palmar interosseous. (Last's p. 109)
The recurrent branch passes superficial to flexor pollicis longus
(Last's p. 111)
The thenar muscles are supplied mainly by C8
Mainly T1 with some C8. (Last's p. 109)
In two-thirds of hands the superficial palmar arch is incomplete
(Last's p. 110)
In the fingers the digital arteries are anterior to the nerves
Nerves are anterior in the fingers; in the palm arteries are superficial. (Last's p. 111)
Common palmar digital nerves divide proximal to the arterial divisions
(Last's p. 110)
Carpal tunnel syndrome causes anaesthesia over the thenar eminence
The palmar branch passes superficial to the retinaculum. (Last's p. 111)
Ulnar-supplied lumbricals are bicipital
Median-supplied lumbricals are unicipital. (Last's p. 112)
Lumbrical tendons pass dorsal to the deep transverse metacarpal ligament
They pass on its palmar surface; interossei pass dorsal. (Last's p. 112, 114)
The deep ulnar branch indents the distal border of the hook of hamate
(Last's p. 114)
The middle finger has a palmar interosseous
It has none; it has two dorsal interossei. (Last's p. 114)

questions.s: Concerning the ulnar nerve in the hand (Last's):
o: The superficial ulnar branch supplies palmaris brevis
(Last's p. 114)
The deep palmar arch lies about 1 cm distal to the superficial arch
It lies about 1 cm proximal. (Last's p. 114)
The first dorsal interosseous may occasionally be supplied by the median
(Last's p. 114)
The deep ulnar branch supplies three lumbricals
Two; the lateral plantar deep branch supplies three. (Last's p. 114)

questions.s: Concerning the sympathetic supply of the upper limb (Last's):
o: Sympathetic fibres to a fingertip arteriole run in the digital nerves
Not along the digital arteries. (Last's p. 122)
Dermatomes C5 and C6 receive grey fibres from the inferior cervical ganglion
From the middle cervical ganglion; C7, 8 from the inferior; T1 from the stellate. (Last's p. 122)
Periarterial sympathectomy denervates only local branches
So it was abandoned. (Last's p. 122)
Upper limb preganglionic fibres come mostly from T1–2 only
Mostly from the upper six thoracic segments. (Last's p. 122)
About 10% of brachial plexuses are prefixed and 10% postfixed
C4–C8 and C6–T2. (Last's p. 122)
C5 fibres of the long thoracic nerve supply the lowest four digitations
C5 upper two, C6 next two, C7 the lowest four. (Last's p. 123)
The suprascapular vessels pass above the transverse scapular ligament
The nerve passes beneath it. (Last's p. 123)
The medial roots of the median nerve join on the medial side of the axillary artery
They join on its lateral side. (Last's p. 123)
The palmar digital branch to the thumb is C6
The recurrent branch is T1. (Last's p. 123)
The median nerve divides into branches distal to the carpal tunnel
Last's says it divides in the carpal tunnel. (Last's p. 123)
The only autonomous median sensory areas are the pulps of index and middle fingers
(Last's p. 127)
In carpal tunnel decompression the retinaculum is cut on the radial side of the nerve
It is cut on the ulnar side to protect the recurrent branch. (Last's p. 127)
The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm is sometimes replaced entirely by the intercostobrachial
Last's calls it "rather a failure". (Last's p. 124)
The lateral and medial cutaneous nerves of the forearm overlap widely at the anterior axial line
They meet without overlap. (Last's p. 124)
The upper-arm part of the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm can be used as a graft
A long length without branches. (Last's p. 124)
The dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve supplies the nail beds
It falls short of the nail beds; the superficial branch supplies them. (Last's p. 124)
The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm carries all the T1 of the radial nerve
With C8. (Last's p. 125)
The lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm is C7
It is C5; the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm is C6, 7. (Last's p. 125)
Last's says radial and dorsal ulnar nerves commonly share the dorsum 2½ : 2½ digits
Rather than the 3½ : 1½ usually quoted. (Last's p. 125)
The posterior interosseous nerve supplies five muscles after leaving supinator
It supplies seven more muscles. (Last's p. 125)
Pectoralis major is the only muscle supplied by all five plexus segments
A guide to the extent of injury. (Last's p. 126)
In Erb's palsy the arm is laterally rotated
It hangs medially rotated, extended at the elbow and pronated. (Last's p. 126)
Radial nerve sensory loss is usually a coin-shaped area over the first dorsal interosseous
(Last's p. 126)
The axillary nerve is damaged in about 25% of shoulder dislocations
About 5%. (Last's p. 126)
A high ulnar lesion gives a less clawed hand than a low one
Ulnar FDP is paralysed. (Last's p. 127)
In median injury the middle finger always stays extended with the index
The middle finger often flexes through FDP connexions or ulnar supply. (Last's p. 127)
Last's advises testing abductor pollicis brevis for low median lesions
Not flexor pollicis brevis. (Last's p. 127)
To display the median nerve in the forearm the ulnar head of FDS is detached
The radial head is detached and the muscle turned medially. (Last's p. 127)
